nameStory: The name "hop trefoil" comes from its resemblance to hops used in brewing beer - the tiny yellow flowers cluster together in rounded heads that look remarkably similar to miniature hop cones. "Lesser" distinguishes it from its larger cousin, the large hop clover, while "trefoil" simply means "three leaves," referring to its classic clover leaflets.
description: Lesser hop trefoil is a small, sprawling clover that forms low mats across the ground. This diminutive member of the pea family grows only 2-8 inches tall, with tiny bright yellow flowers clustered in round heads about the size of a pencil eraser. Its three-part leaves are classic clover shape but much smaller than most other clovers you'll encounter. Despite its small stature, it's quite common and often carpets areas in golden yellow during its blooming period.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers packed into dense, rounded heads about 1/4 inch across that look like miniature golden pom-poms; flowers eventually turn brown and papery, creating a hop-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic three-leaflet clover leaves but noticeably small - each leaflet is only about 1/4 to 1/2 inch long with a heart-shaped or oval form and often a tiny notch at the tip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant that rarely exceeds 8 inches tall, often forming dense mats; stems feel soft and slightly hairy when you run your fingers along them

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, the dried flower heads remain attached and turn brown, resembling tiny dried hops; these persistent brown clusters help identify the plant even when not in bloom

habitat: Lesser hop trefoil thrives in disturbed areas with poor, sandy, or gravelly soil where other plants struggle. Look for it in parking lot edges, along sidewalks, in thin lawns, vacant lots, and roadside areas throughout New England. It particularly loves sunny spots with compacted or nutrient-poor soil that larger plants can't colonize.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of three-part leaves, often forming dense patches in areas where snow has melted early.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flower heads appear from late spring through summer, creating golden carpets in suitable habitat; this is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers turn brown and papery, creating the characteristic hop-like appearance; plants may continue growing in mild weather.
seasonality.winter: Plants typically die back, leaving only dried stems and seed heads in protected areas; new plants will germinate from seed in spring.

funFact: This humble little plant is widely accepted as the true shamrock of Ireland! While many people think of larger clovers as shamrocks, lesser hop trefoil is actually the species most commonly associated with St. Patrick's Day traditions and Irish folklore.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large hop clover, but lesser hop trefoil's flower heads are much smaller (pencil eraser vs. marble size) and the whole plant stays under 8 inches tall. Memory trick: "Lesser" means smaller flowers, shorter height - everything about it is more petite than its hop clover cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "trefoil," this is actually a true clover in the genus Trifolium. The term "trefoil" technically just means "three leaves" and can apply to any three-leaflet plant, but in common usage it often refers to the smaller, yellow-flowered clovers like this species.
compareHints: Among New England's clovers, lesser hop trefoil stands out for its tiny size and bright yellow flowers - most other clovers have white, pink, or red blooms. Large hop clover looks similar but is significantly larger in all parts, while white and red clovers have completely different colored flowers and grow much taller. The small stature and golden color make lesser hop trefoil quite distinctive once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's clovers, red clover is the tallest and most upright, while white clover creeps along the ground and has white flowers.
Among New England clovers, white clover is unique for its creeping growth habit and pure white spherical flowers.

Among New England clovers, rabbitfoot clover is unique for its fuzzy, pale, cylindrical flower heads - completely different from the round pink heads of red clover, the round white heads of white clover, or the small yellow clusters of hop clovers.
Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, large hop clover stands tallest and most erect, while hop trefoil sprawls closer to the ground with smaller flowers.

Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, hop trefoil stands out with its distinctive oval, hop-shaped flower heads compared to the round heads of large hop clover or the tiny heads of lesser hop trefoil.
Among New England's clovers, alsike is the tall one with color-changing flowers.
Crimson clover stands out from other New England clovers by its distinctive torpedo-shaped, brilliant red flower heads - no other local clover has this intense crimson color or elongated cone shape.
Zigzag clover differs from red clover by having narrower leaflets without white markings and distinctive angled stems.
